content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The entry's core—gnashing as the rage of the wicked at the righteous, provoked by the sight of the kingdom from which they are excluded—is carried directly by the printed references. Luke 13:28 explicitly conditions the gnashing on a sight ('when ye shall see Abraham... and you yourselves thrust out'), matching the entry's trigger. Every non-Gospel occurrence supplied (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Acts 7:54; and the chapter's additional Job 16:9, Ps 35:16, Lam 2:16) uses gnashing exclusively as hostility directed at a righteous party, never as a sound of self-directed pain. Ps 112:10 supplies the entry's full printed sequence—sees, grieved (grief), gnashes (hatred/gnashing), melts away and perishes (destruction)—and Acts 7:54 stages the same tableau in narrative: the council gnashing while the righteous man sees heaven opened. The strongest counter (mainstream anguish-of-the-damned reading) cannot account for the uniform hostile usage of the term across the Hebrew Bible and Acts without positing an unexplained semantic shift inside the Matthean formula, and it must read past Luke 13:28's explicit sight-trigger. The book's core reading is itself a recognized 'common' alternative in three of the four blinded responses, drawn from exactly these texts. No supplied text is inexplicable on the book's core; the counter's remaining texts (the other Matthean occurrences) are equally compatible with the book's reading. Every material assertion actually printed in the entry is supported by the printed references, so the scope is FULL.","book_core_identification":"Gnashing of teeth is the rage/hatred of the wicked directed at the righteous, occurring especially when the excluded see the kingdom and the blessed within it—an other-directed hostile reaction, not primarily the self-directed anguish or torment-noise of the condemned.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The gnashing scene includes a sequence of grief, hatred, gnashing, and destruction (supported by Ps 112:10: sees, grieved, gnashes, melts away, perishes).","This sequence follows an established pattern found in the Psalms (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12) and in Stephen's accusers (Acts 7:54)."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":[],"chapter_only_objections":["The claim that the Greek definite articles ('the weeping and the gnashing') mark a known fixed scene is a philological argument made only in the chapter and is not verifiable from the supplied KJV excerpts.","The appeal to a 'Hebrew Matthew' rendering (charaq; Gehinnom; lowest Sheol; dark places of the depths) rests on an extra-canonical textual witness not supplied in the evidence excerpts.","The chapter's stronger annihilationist inference—that the gnasher 'melts away' in all seven Gospel occurrences and that the formula never describes inflicted torments—generalizes Ps 112:10's ending beyond what the Gospel texts state.","The claim that in all seven occurrences the one cast out is an insider/claimant depends on readings of Matthean texts (13:41-42, 13:49-50, 22:13, 24:51, 25:30) not printed with the glossary entry."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The mainstream reading: 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' is a fixed formula for the extreme anguish, despair, and remorse of the condemned under eschatological punishment—self-directed suffering at exclusion and torment, with the gnashing expressing pain or bitter regret rather than hostility aimed at the righteous.","counter_core_identification":"Gnashing of teeth symbolizes the conscious anguish and remorseful despair of the damned experiencing judgment and exclusion—an inward reaction to their own suffering and loss, not rage directed at the blessed.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that the gnashing is other-directed hostility at the righteous, asserting instead that it is self-directed anguish/remorse under punishment; both cannot be the primary identification of the same symbol, since the book expressly reads the gnashing as hatred aimed at those inside the kingdom rather than as the register of the excluded party's own torment.","counter_case":["The formula is paired with 'weeping,' which naturally suggests sorrow and anguish rather than aggression.","The settings—outer darkness, furnace of fire—are punishment scenes, so the natural referent of the reaction is the punishment itself.","The formula's stereotyped sevenfold repetition suggests a stock idiom of eschatological misery rather than a precise emotional analysis.","This is the dominant reading across mainstream Christian teaching and all four blinded responses' primary meanings."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Uniform lexical usage: every supplied occurrence of gnashing outside the Matthean formula (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Acts 7:54; plus Job 16:9, Ps 35:16, Lam 2:16 in the chapter) is hostility aimed at a righteous party—never a pain response—so the book reads the word consistently across the whole canon.","Luke 13:28 explicitly ties the gnashing to a sight ('when ye shall see' the patriarchs in the kingdom and yourselves thrust out), which matches the entry's trigger and which the anguish reading must treat as incidental.","Ps 112:10 reproduces the entry's whole printed sequence in one verse: the wicked sees, is grieved, gnashes, and melts away—grief, hatred, gnashing, destruction.","Acts 7:54 provides a narrative enactment of the identical scene: the wicked gnashing at a righteous man as he sees the opened heaven, confirming the pattern in New Testament usage.","The book still accounts for 'weeping' via the grief element (Ps 112:10 'be grieved'), so it explains both halves of the formula rather than only one."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Fits the intuitive reading of 'weeping' as sorrow and the punitive settings (furnace, darkness) as contexts of suffering.","Matches the majority tradition and requires no reclassification of the familiar formula."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Psalms 112:10","Luke 13:28","Acts 7:54","Psalms 37:12","Matthew 8:12"],"unresolved_objections":["The Matthean occurrences other than Matt 8:12 (13:42, 13:50, 22:13, 24:51, 25:30) place the formula inside overt punishment imagery (furnace of fire), and while compatible with the book's reading, they do not by themselves specify the direction of the gnashing.","The pairing with 'weeping' keeps the mainstream anguish register plausible as a component of the scene, though the entry itself already incorporates grief and so is not defeated by it."],"confidence":"high"}
